hello.title: Hello, Java
hello.summary: Write your first Java program with a class, a main method and System.out.println, and learn how to compile and run it.
hello.lesson.0: Java programs are made of **classes**. A class is a named block of code. Every program needs at least one class; here it is called `Main`. Inside the class, the program starts in a **method** called `main`. Curly braces `{ }` mark where a block begins and where it ends.
hello.lesson.2: The line `public static void main(String[] args)` is the same in every program. For now, copy it as it is. You learn what `public`, `static`, `void` and `String[] args` mean later in this course. `System.out.println` prints the value in the parentheses and then starts a new line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello"`, is a **string**.
hello.lesson.3: Every instruction is called a **statement** and ends with a semicolon `;`. `System.out.print` (without `ln`) prints without starting a new line, so the next output continues on the same line. Java is **case-sensitive**: `System` and `system` are different names, and only `System` works.
hello.lesson.6: You save the code in a file that ends in `.java`. A `public class` must be in a file with the same name, so the class `Main` goes into `Main.java`. The command `javac Main.java` **compiles** the code: it checks it for errors and translates it into a file called `Main.class`. Then `java Main` runs the program. If the code has an error, `javac` reports it and nothing runs.
hello.lesson.7: Since Java 11, the command `java Main.java` compiles and runs a single file in one step. This is handy for small programs like the ones in this course.
hello.lesson.9: Numbers do not need quotes. Java calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). It calculates the result first and then prints it. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses come first.
hello.lesson.11: When you divide two whole numbers with `/`, Java drops the rest: `7 / 2` is `3`. The operator `%` gives you the rest of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`. Write `7.0 / 2` to get a result with decimals: `3.5`.
hello.lesson.13: `"5"` with quotes is a string, `5` without quotes is a number. For strings, `+` joins the text: `"2" + "3"` gives `23`, but `2 + 3` gives `5`.
hello.card.1: `public static void main(String[] args) { }` is where it starts
hello.card.2: `System.out.println(x);` prints `x` and a new line, `print` does not
hello-1.prompt: Which line prints Hello and then starts a new line?
hello-1.explain: `System.out.println` prints the string and starts a new line. `print` stays on the same line, `println` alone does not exist, and text needs double quotes.
hello-3.explain: `17` divided by `5` is `3` with a rest of `2`. The operator `%` gives the rest.

hello-4.options.3: `A` and then `BC` on the next line
hello-4.explain: `print` does not start a new line, so `B` follows `A` directly. `println("B")` ends the line, and `C` comes on the next one.
hello-5.statement: The class `public class Main` must be saved in a file called `Main.java`.
hello-5.explain: A `public class` must be in a file with the same name as the class, plus `.java`.
hello-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints Hi.
hello-6.explain: Java prints with `System.out.println` (or `print`). `echo`, `printLine` and `say` do not exist.
hello-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 3.5.
hello-7.explain: `7 / 2` divides two whole numbers and gives `3`. With `7.0` the result has decimals: `3.5`.
hello-8.prompt: Build a statement that prints the result of 6 times 7.
hello-8.explain: `System.out.println(6 * 7);` calculates `6 * 7` first and prints `42`. The statement ends with `;`.

hello-9.explain: The class contains `main`, and `main` contains the statements. `print("Ja")` stays on the line, `println("va")` completes `Java` and ends the line, then `Done` follows.

variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables and meet the types int, double, boolean, char and String, plus var and final.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. In Java, every variable has a **type** that says what kind of value it holds. You write the type, the name, `=` and the value: `int age = 30;`. Here `=` means "store", not "is equal to".
variables.lesson.2: To change a variable, assign a new value without the type: `score = score + 5;` takes the old value, adds `5` and stores the result. `score += 3;` is a short form of `score = score + 3;`. `score++;` adds `1`, and `score--;` subtracts `1`.
variables.lesson.5: `int` holds whole numbers, `double` holds numbers with decimals, and `boolean` holds `true` or `false`. `char` holds one single character in single quotes, like `'A'`. `String` holds text in double quotes. It starts with a capital `S` because it is a class, not a basic type.
variables.lesson.7: Java checks the types when it compiles. A `String` never fits into an `int` variable. An `int` fits into a `double`: `double x = 7;` stores `7.0`. A `double` does not fit into an `int` on its own. You need a **cast**: `(int) 3.9` cuts off the decimals and gives `3`.
variables.lesson.10: With `var`, Java finds the type from the value: `var count = 5;` creates an `int`. The type is still fixed, so `count` can never hold a `String` later. You can use `var` only for variables inside a method that get a value right away.
variables.lesson.11: A variable marked `final` cannot change after it gets its value. If you try, the program does not compile. Names of such constants are often written in capital letters with `_` between the words, like `MAX_SPEED`.
variables.lesson.13: From now on, short code in the exercises often shows only the lines inside `main`, or only the parts inside the class. To run such code, you put it into a full program like the ones above.
variables.card.0: `int age = 30;` creates a variable with a type
variables.card.4: `var n = 5;` finds the type, `final` makes it constant
variables-1.prompt: Which line creates a variable for a whole number?
variables-1.explain: First the type `int`, then the name, then `=` and the value. `"30"` is a string, and `Int` with a capital letter is not a Java type.
variables-2.explain: `x` starts at `5`, becomes `8`, and `x *= 2` doubles it to `16`.
variables-3.explain: The cast `(int)` cuts off the decimals. It does not round, so `9.99` becomes `9`.
variables-4.explain: The `int` value `4` fits into a `double` and becomes `4.0`. A `double` always prints with a decimal point.
variables-5.statement: A variable created with `var` can later hold a value of a different type.
variables-5.explain: `var` only saves you from writing the type. Java still gives the variable a fixed type, so `var x = 5;` followed by `x = "five";` does not compile.
variables-6.prompt: Fill the gap so that the value of RATE can never change.
variables-6.explain: `final` makes a variable constant. `var double` is not valid, `const` is not used in Java, and `static` is not allowed for a variable inside a method.
variables-7.prompt: Fill the gap with the right type.
variables-7.explain: Single quotes hold one `char`. A `String` needs double quotes, and `Char` and `string` are not Java types.
variables-8.prompt: Build a statement that creates a variable price with the value 9.5.
variables-8.explain: `9.5` has decimals, so the type is `double`. An `int` cannot hold it, and `"9.5"` is a string.
variables-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints 12.
variables-9.explain: `n` starts at `2`, times `5` is `10`, plus `2` is `12`. The other way round, you get `(2 + 2) * 5`, which is `20`.
variables-10.prompt: Match the type with what it holds.
variables-11.explain: `4.99` has decimals and does not fit into an `int`. Write `double price = 4.99;`.
variables-12.explain: Single quotes are for one `char`. A `String` needs double quotes: `String name = "Ana";`.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Join strings with +, work with length, charAt, substring and toUpperCase, and compare text with equals.
strings.lesson.0: The operator `+` joins strings. This is called **concatenation**. When one side is a string and the other side is a number, Java turns the number into text first.
strings.lesson.2: Java reads `+` from left to right. `"Sum: " + 2 + 3` first gives `"Sum: 2"` and then `"Sum: 23"`. Use parentheses to calculate first: `"Sum: " + (2 + 3)`. In `2 + 3 + " apples"`, the numbers come first, so Java adds them.
strings.lesson.5: A string has **methods**: actions you call with a dot and parentheses. `word.length()` gives the number of characters. `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` give a new string in capital or small letters. The original string never changes: strings in Java are **immutable**.
strings.lesson.7: Every character has a position, called its **index**. The index starts at `0`. `charAt(i)` gives the `char` at index `i`. `substring(start, end)` gives the characters from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. `substring(start)` goes to the end of the string.
strings.lesson.9: The last index is `length() - 1`. `"Hello".charAt(5)` stops the program with an error called `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
strings.lesson.11: To check if two strings contain the same text, use `a.equals(b)`. It gives `true` or `false`. Do not use `==` for strings: it checks if both names point to the very same object in memory. Two strings with the same text can be different objects. `equalsIgnoreCase` compares and ignores capital and small letters.
strings.card.2: `s.charAt(0)` is the first character, the index starts at `0`
strings-1.explain: Java reads from left to right. `"Total: " + 4` is a string, so `5` is joined as text: `Total: 45`.
strings-3.explain: The index starts at `0`: `P` is `0`, `l` is `1`, and `a` is `2`.
strings-5.explain: Strings never change. `toUpperCase()` returns a new string, but the code does not store it, so `s` is still `Java`.
strings-6.prompt: Which expression checks if the strings a and b contain the same text?
strings-6.explain: `equals` compares the text. `==` checks if both are the same object, `=` stores a value, and `same` does not exist.
strings-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the code prints Ann.
strings-7.explain: `substring(0, 3)` gives index `0` to `2`: `Ann`. `charAt` takes only one index, and `slice` and `sub` do not exist for Java strings.
strings-8.prompt: Which line has the bug? The code should print the last letter.
strings-8.explain: The last index is `length() - 1`. Write `word.charAt(word.length() - 1)`; `charAt(word.length())` stops with an error.
strings-9.prompt: Build a statement that joins first and last with a space between them.
strings-9.explain: `+` joins strings. `" "` is a string with one space, so `full` becomes `Ada King`.
strings-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints NANA 4.
strings-10.explain: Each line uses the variable from the line before: `substring(2)` gives `nana`, `toUpperCase()` gives `NANA`, and `NANA` has `4` characters.

strings-12.prompt: Which line has the bug? The code should print true.

conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Make decisions with if and else, comparison and logical operators, switch expressions and the ternary operator.
conditions.lesson.0: An `if` statement runs a block of code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses `( )`, the code in curly braces `{ }`. After the block, the program continues as normal.
conditions.lesson.2: Comparisons give a `boolean`: `==` (equal to), `!=` (not equal to), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` (less than or equal to) and `>=` (greater than or equal to). Do not mix up `==` and `=`: `=` stores a value, `==` compares two values.
conditions.lesson.5: The block after `else` runs when the condition is `false`. With `else if` you can test more conditions. Java checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is `true`.
conditions.lesson.7: **Logical operators** combine conditions. `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are `true`. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
conditions.lesson.10: A `switch` expression picks a value depending on another value. Each `case` lists one or more values, then an arrow `->` and the result. `default` covers all other values. Because the whole `switch` gives a value, a semicolon follows the closing brace.
conditions.lesson.12: The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` is a short `if` that gives a value: `a` when the condition is `true`, otherwise `b`.
conditions-1.explain: `8 > 5` is `true`, so the first block runs.
conditions-2.explain: `15 > 20` is `false`, but `15 > 10` is `true`. Java runs only that block and skips the `else`.
conditions-3.explain: `a > 2` is `true`, but `b < 5` is `false`. `&&` needs both sides to be `true`.
conditions-4.explain: `=` stores a value; it does not compare. For an `int`, `if (x = 5)` does not even compile. Write `if (x == 5)`.
conditions-5.explain: No `case` matches `4`, so `default` gives the value `?`.
conditions-6.explain: `15 >= 18` is `false`, so the ternary operator gives the value after the `:`.
conditions-7.prompt: Fill the gap so that Enter is printed only when both conditions are true.
conditions-7.explain: `&&` is `true` only when both sides are `true`. With `||`, one `true` side is enough. `and` is not a Java operator.
conditions-8.prompt: Fill the gap to complete the switch expression.
conditions-8.explain: In a `switch` expression, each `case` uses the arrow `->` before its value.
conditions-9.prompt: Build a statement that stores positive when n is greater than 0, otherwise negative.
conditions-9.explain: The ternary operator is `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`. It does not use `if` or `else`.
conditions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints Hot.
conditions-10.explain: The variable comes first. `30 > 25` is `true`, so the block right after the `if` must print `Hot`.

conditions-11.pairs.3: at least one must be true
conditions-12.explain: A second condition needs `else if`. Write `} else if (age >= 13) {`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for, while and do-while loops, go through arrays with the enhanced for, and use break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop repeats a block of code. Its header has three parts, separated by semicolons: the start (`int i = 1`), the condition (`i <= 3`) and the update (`i++`). Java runs the block as long as the condition is `true` and does the update after each round.
loops.lesson.2: The update can be anything that changes the variable. `i += 5` counts in steps of five, and `i--` counts down. A variable outside the loop can collect a result, for example a sum.
loops.lesson.5: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. It checks the condition before each round. Make sure that something in the block changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.7: A `do-while` loop runs the block first and checks the condition after it. So the block always runs at least once. Note the semicolon after `while (...)`.
loops.lesson.10: An **array** holds several values of the same type: `String[] names = {"Ana", "Ben"};`. The unit about arrays and lists explains them in detail. The enhanced `for` loop goes through all values: read `for (String name : names)` as "for each `name` in `names`".
loops.lesson.12: `break` ends a loop right away. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.
loops.card.3: `for (String s : names) { }` goes through all values
loops.card.4: `break` ends the loop, `continue` skips a round
loops-1.explain: `i` starts at `0` and the loop runs while `i < 4`, so it prints `0`, `1`, `2` and `3` on one line.
loops-3.prompt: How many times does this code print Hi?
loops-3.explain: `i` takes the values `2`, `4` and `6`. At `8`, the condition `i < 8` is `false`.
loops-4.explain: `n` goes `100`, `50`, `25`, `12`, `6`. Dividing whole numbers drops the rest, so `25 / 2` is `12`. At `6`, `n > 10` is `false`.
loops-5.statement: A `do-while` loop runs its block at least once, even when the condition is `false` from the start.
loops-5.explain: `do-while` checks the condition only after the block, so the block runs once before the first check.
loops-6.explain: When `i` is `4`, `break` ends the loop before the `print`. So only `1`, `2` and `3` are printed.
loops-7.explain: `continue` skips the `print` for `3` and `6`, which can be divided by `3`.
loops-8.prompt: Fill the gap so the code prints the numbers 1 to 5.
loops-8.explain: `i <= 5` includes `5`. With `<` the loop stops at `4`, with `>=` it never runs, and `=>` is not a Java operator.
loops-9.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop goes through all numbers in the array.
loops-9.explain: The enhanced `for` loop uses a colon: `for (int n : numbers)`. `in` and `of` are used in other languages, not in Java.
loops-10.prompt: Build a loop header that counts 0, 1, 2.
loops-10.explain: The three parts of the header are separated by semicolons: start `int i = 0`, condition `i < 3`, update `i++`.
loops-11.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints 3, 2, 1 on separate lines and then Go!
loops-11.explain: Inside the loop, print `i` first and then count down. `Go!` comes after the loop, so it is printed once.
loops-12.explain: A `do-while` loop ends with a semicolon. Write `} while (n < 3);`.
methods.title: Methods
methods.summary: Write your own static methods with parameters and return values, and overload a method for different types.
methods.lesson.0: A **method** is a named block of code that you can run again and again by calling its name. `main` is a method too. You write your own methods inside the class, next to `main`. For now, start each one with `static`. The word `void` means that the method gives no result back.
methods.lesson.2: A method can take **parameters**: values it gets from the caller. You list them in the parentheses, each with a type and a name, separated by commas. When you call the method, you pass the values, called **arguments**, in the same order.
methods.lesson.5: Instead of `void`, you can write the type of a result, for example `int`. Then the method must end with `return` and a value of that type. `return` sends the value back to the caller, which can store it, print it or calculate with it.
methods.lesson.7: `return` ends the method right away. So a method can return early from inside an `if`, and the code after it does not run.
methods.lesson.9: A parameter is a copy of the argument. If a method changes its parameter, the variable of the caller stays the same. Variables you create inside a method exist only in that method.
methods.lesson.12: Several methods can have the same name if their parameters are different: a different number of parameters or different types. This is called **overloading**. Java picks the method whose parameters match the arguments.
methods.card.1: `static int square(int n) { return n * n; }`
methods.card.2: `square(4)` calls the method with the argument `4`
methods.card.3: `return` ends the method and gives back a value
methods-2.explain: The loop runs three times and adds `ab` each time, so the method returns `ababab`.
methods-3.prompt: What does `void` mean in `static void greet()`?
methods-3.options.0: The method gives no value back.
methods-3.options.3: The method can run only once.
methods-3.explain: `void` is the return type for "nothing". The empty parentheses `()` are what show that there are no parameters.
methods-4.explain: `2.0` has a decimal point, so it is a `double`. Java picks the overloaded method with a `double` parameter.
methods-5.explain: The parameter `n` is a copy of `x`. Changing `n` does not change `x`, so the code prints `1`.
methods-6.explain: `7 % 2` is `1`, so `n % 2 == 0` is `false`, and the method returns `false`.

methods-7.explain: `w * h` is an `int`, so the return type is `int`. A `void` method cannot return a value, and an `int` is not a `String`.

methods-8.explain: `return a;` sends `a` back and ends the method, so `return b;` does not run.

methods-9.explain: First `static`, then the return type `double`, the name `half` and the parameter `double x` in parentheses.

methods-10.explain: With `70` points, the `if` returns `pass` and the method ends. With `20`, the `if` block is skipped and the method returns `fail`.

collections.title: Arrays and lists
collections.summary: Store many values in arrays and ArrayLists, read and change them by index, and go through them with loops.
collections.lesson.0: An **array** holds a fixed number of values of the same type. `int[] scores = {90, 75, 82};` creates an array with three `int` values: `[]` after the type means "array of". You read a value by its index in square brackets, starting at `0`: `scores[0]`. You change it with `scores[1] = 80;`.
collections.lesson.2: `scores.length` gives the size of an array, without parentheses. `new int[3]` creates an array with three zeros. To print a whole array, use `Arrays.toString`. It is in the package `java.util`, so the file needs the line `import java.util.Arrays;` before the class.
collections.lesson.4: You can go through an array with a counting `for` loop, from `0` to `length - 1`, or with the enhanced `for` loop. Use the counting loop when you need the index.
collections.lesson.6: The last index is `length - 1`. An index outside the array stops the program with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
collections.lesson.7: Now you can read `String[] args` in `main`: it is an array of strings. It holds the words you type after `java Main` on the command line.
collections.lesson.9: An array cannot grow. An `ArrayList` can. `ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` creates an empty list of strings: the type of the values goes in angle brackets `< >`, and `new` creates the list. Its methods are `add`, `get`, `set`, `remove`, `size` and `contains`. It needs `import java.util.ArrayList;`.
collections.lesson.11: Lists hold objects, so for numbers you write `Integer` instead of `int` (and `Double` instead of `double`). `List.of(4, 8, 15)` creates a short list in one step. The type `List<Integer>` and `List.of` need `import java.util.List;`. The enhanced `for` loop works with lists too.
collections.lesson.13: A list from `List.of` cannot change. Calling `add` on it stops the program with an `UnsupportedOperationException`. If you need to change it, make an `ArrayList` copy: `new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2))`.
collections.card.4: `for (int n : numbers) { }` goes through all values

collections-2.explain: `a.length` is `3`, and `a[2]` is the last value, `9`. `3 + 9` is `12`.

collections-5.explain: A list from `List.of` cannot change. `add` stops the program with an `UnsupportedOperationException`.
collections-6.prompt: Which line creates an empty list for whole numbers?
collections-6.explain: Lists hold objects, so the type is `Integer`, not `int`. And `new` is needed to create the list.
collections-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the code prints Ana.
collections-7.explain: `get(0)` returns the value at index `0` of a list. `charAt` is a method of strings, not of lists.
collections-8.prompt: Fill the gap so the loop goes through the whole array.
collections-8.explain: An array has `length` without parentheses. `length()` is for strings, and `size()` is for lists.
collections-9.prompt: Build a statement that creates an array colors with red and blue, in this order.
collections-9.explain: The type `String[]` means an array of strings. The values go in curly braces, separated by commas.

classes.title: Classes and records
classes.summary: Create your own types with classes, fields, constructors and methods, and hold data in short records.
classes.lesson.0: A class is a plan for your own type. **Fields** are the variables that each object of the class has. You create an **object** with `new`, and you reach its fields with a dot.
classes.lesson.2: Here the class `Dog` is in the same file as `Main`, before it. Only one class in a file can be `public`. In bigger projects, each class has its own file. Fields that you do not set get a default value: `0` for numbers and `false` for `boolean`.
classes.lesson.4: A **constructor** sets up a new object. It has the same name as the class and no return type, and it runs when you call `new`. Inside it, `this` means the object being created: `this.name` is the field, and `name` alone is the parameter.
classes.lesson.6: Methods without `static` belong to an object. You call them on an object with a dot, like `acc.deposit(50)`, and they can read and change the fields of that object. A `static` method belongs to the class itself and needs no object. That is why `main` is `static`.
classes.lesson.8: `public` means that all classes can use something. In real projects, fields are often `private`, like `private double balance;`. Then only the class itself can use them, and other code must call its methods.
classes.lesson.10: A **record** is a short way to write a class that only holds data: `record Point(int x, int y) {}`. Java creates the fields, the constructor and a method for each value, like `p.x()`. A record also prints in a readable form, `equals` compares the values, and the values cannot change.
classes.lesson.12: If you print an object of a normal class, you get something like `Dog@1b6d3586`, the class name and a code. Records print their values instead.
classes.card.1: `Dog(String name) { this.name = name; }` is a constructor
classes.card.2: `Dog d = new Dog("Rex");` creates an object
classes.card.3: `d.bark()` calls a method on the object
classes-1.explain: `count` starts at `0`. The two calls of `add` change the field of the same object: `0 + 5 + 2` is `7`.
classes-2.explain: A record creates a method for each value: `name()` returns `Tea` and `price()` returns `2.5`.
classes-3.options.0: It creates a new object of the class `Dog`.
classes-3.options.1: It creates a new class called `Dog`.
classes-3.options.2: It changes the name of every `Dog` object.
classes-3.explain: `new` creates an object and runs the constructor with the argument `"Rex"`. The class must already exist.
classes-4.explain: Each object has its own fields. Changing `a.name` does not change `b.name`.
classes-5.statement: A constructor needs a return type, for example `void`.
classes-5.explain: A constructor has the name of the class and no return type. With `void` in front, it becomes a normal method and is no longer a constructor.
classes-6.explain: A record prints its name and its values in square brackets.
classes-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the constructor stores the name in the field.
classes-7.explain: `this.name` is the field of the new object, and `name` is the parameter. Java uses `this`, not `self`.
classes-8.prompt: Fill the gap to create a Point object.
classes-8.explain: `new` creates an object, for classes and for records.
classes-9.prompt: Build a record Book with a String title and an int pages, in this order.
classes-9.explain: A record lists its values in parentheses after the name, followed by a body in curly braces, here empty.
classes-10.prompt: There is a record Point(int x, int y). Put the lines in order so the code prints Point[x=4, y=2].
classes-10.explain: `moved` uses the values of `start`, so `start` comes first. `1 + 3` is `4`, and `y` stays `2`.
classes-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
classes-11.pairs.3: a short class that holds data
classes-12.prompt: Which line has the bug? new Box(5).size should be 5.
classes-12.explain: `size = size;` stores the parameter in itself, so the field stays `0`. Write `this.size = size;`.
